sbh1.2:1.0: The avatārabhūmi opens by enumerating the six person-types it will define: *bhavya* (merely fit), the three grades of wholesome roots (mild, middle, strong), *niṣṭhā-prāyogika* (applied to the ultimate), and *niṣṭhā-gata* (arrived at the ultimate). Sections 1.4–1.27 define each in turn.
sbh1.2:1.1: The opening enumeration is six person-types/stages, not six independent factors: merely fit, mild/middle/strong wholesome roots, applied to the ultimate, and arrived at the ultimate. The wording is kept aligned with the structural overview and the definitions that follow.
sbh1.2:1.9: *yāvat dṛṣṭi-ṛjū-kṛtā* — the Sanskrit *yāvat* signals 'as elaborated above, up to the point of ...'. Standard Buddhist-text shorthand: the full description from the *bhavya* entry above is implied, repeated in summary by the trailing milestone (here, 'making the view upright').
sbh1.2:1.18: *ātmabhāva-pratilambha* — 'attainment of [the final] individual existence.' Refers to the body-and-mind continuum that becomes the substrate for the path's culmination. The 'final' here means *carama-* (last in the saṁsāric series for this person), not chronologically late in life.
sbh1.2:1.20: The root text as extracted prints *āsrava-kṣayam anuprāpnoti* ('attains the destruction of the fluxes'), but that would make the *niṣṭhā-prāyogika* an arhat and collapse the contrast with the immediately following *niṣṭhā-gata*. The recapitulation at 2.9–2.13 explicitly says this person realizes stream-entry, once-returning, or non-returning but not arhatship. The English therefore restores the required negative sense and marks the line [Damaged/Conjectural]; Sanskrit JSON is left unchanged.
sbh1.2:1.26: *paramaśītī-bhāva-prāpta* — literally 'attained the supreme state of becoming-cool.' Coolness (*śīta*) is the standard Buddhist metaphor for nirvāṇa, contrasting with the burning of the kleśas. Rendered 'supreme calming' for English readability; 'supreme cooling' or 'highest peace' would also work.
sbh1.2:4.1: Restructured as a single question across 4.1–4.3 — the source uses three short *|*-separated clauses (asking about fixed measure, equal duration, and certainty respectively) that together form one question whose answer is given in 4.4. Punctuation here makes that visible.
sbh1.2:4.15: Sections 4.15–4.25 describe the descended person's distinctive *first mark* through a two-part contrast: 4.16–4.19 — rejection of an ill-stated dharma even when praised; 4.20 — simile for the un-descended state, where one cannot connect with even the well-stated dharma (like a honey-creature thrown into vinegar); 4.21–4.24 — the descended person's positive embrace of the well-stated dharma (like a honey-creature in honey). The contrast is the *mark* — what distinguishes the descended from the un-descended is precisely this changed orientation toward dharma.
sbh1.2:4.20: *svākhyātasya … dharmavinayasya* — 'of the well-stated dharma-vinaya.' Counterintuitive in context (the descended person is supposed to *embrace* the well-stated), but coherent if read as describing the *un-descended* state to which the simile compares: the un-descended person, like a honey-creature thrown into vinegar, cannot survive in the well-stated dharma until descent has occurred. 4.21 then turns to the post-descent positive case.
sbh1.2:9.3: Read the closing descriptors as *nihata-mada-māna-ahaṁkāraḥ, guṇa-abhiniviṣṭaḥ, doṣa-dveṣṭā*: conceit, pride, and egotism are struck down; the practitioner is intent on good qualities and averse to faults. The earlier reading treated *guṇa-abhiniviṣṭa* as part of what was struck down and emended *doṣa-dveṣṭā* toward *a-doṣa/a-dveṣṭā*; the transmitted wording makes better sense as positive ethical orientation.
